newsitem.title: USA: Dow cracks 6,600 mark, shrugging off higher rates.
newsitem.headline: Dow cracks 6,600 mark, shrugging off higher rates.

text.p: U.S. stocks cracked the milestone 6600-level on the Dow industrials on Tuesday but a soft bond market could be a signal of near-term volatility for Wall Street.

The record-breaking bull market showed its resilience during the session, turning around from a 55-point Dow decline to post a 33-point gain, despite rising interest rates in the bond market, analysts said.
"The bull market is alive and well," Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards and Sons.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended up 33.48 points to a record 6600.66.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond finished off 7/32, its yield rising to 6.79 percent from Monday's close at 6.77 percent.
While analysts said the latest century mark on the Dow did not hold great technical significance, the manner in which stocks reached the mark did raise some eyebrows.
"If rates are going up...how can this market turn this negative into a positive?" said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
"This market has been fueled by the jet fuel of lower interest rates," he added.
Bleier noted that low interest rates have been a key leg to the bull market, along with slow economic growth, strong corporate earnings and the steady flow of investor funds.

The Dow rose 26 percent in 1996. Few on Wall Street expect a repeat in 1997, with most market watchers predicting slower corporate earnings growth and market volatility to keep the growth closer to eight-to-10 percent.

Interest rates in the bond market rose on Tuesday amid concern upcoming data may show a stronger-than-expected U.S. economy, which some believe could lead to a Federal Reserve hike in interest rates next month.
Thursday brings a report on December producer prices and Friday December nonfarm payrolls data. Strong numbers could spark sharp reactions in both bonds and stocks, analysts said.
A continued rise in interest rates will eventually drive investors out of stocks, but that point has not been reached yet, said Gregory Nie, a technical analyst at EVEREN Securities.
Improving corporate earnings fueled by a stronger economy will offset slowly rising rates, Nie said.
"It looks like stocks can navigate gradually rising interest rates," he said.
